newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe war veterans vow to continue protests.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe war veterans vow to continue protests.

text.p: Zimbabwe's independence war veterans, who looted the headquarters of President Robert Mugabe's ruling ZANU-PF party, vowed on Thursday to press ahead in their campaign for compensation payments.

The official daily Herald newspaper said about 100 ex-combatants ransacked the party offices in Harare on Wednesday night, cutting telephone lines, looting food and cigarettes and briefly holding some office workers hostage.

Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association chairman Chenjerai Hunzvi urged Mugabe's government to meet the ex-fighters' demands for unconditional resumption of war victims' compensation payments suspended in March.
"The ex-combatants are very much disgruntled because they are living a destitute life and you cannot give excuses that they must be loyal," Hunzvi was quoted as saying by state news agency ZIANA.
"Arrests will only provoke resentment ... The politicians should be the first to know that people were detained, sent to prison during the colonial times, but did that stop the uprisings?"
He was referring to reports by the Herald newspaper that acting police commissioner Godwin Matanga had instructed his officers to arrest some of the veterans who stormed the party headquarters.
It was the latest incident in a campaign by the veterans -- heroes of a 1970s guerrilla war that won the southern African state independence in 1980 -- to win compensation from the government.
The government suspended the general war victims' compensation fund in March to ease investigations into charges the fund had been heavily defrauded, including by some cabinet members.
Mugabe has set up a judicial commission to probe the charges, and his government is only paying out compensation on a slow, case-by-case basis.

The ex-fighters have staged a series of spectacular protests around the country in the last two months, demanding unconditional release of their claims and a meeting with Mugabe, who is patron of their association.
Mugabe says he will only meet them when he has "the full facts", but Hunzvi called for an early meeting, saying the ex-combatants had waited too long.
